reason: jpeg.rb:347-350 reads the declared segment length, checks only data[0,5]=="JFIF\0", then calls data[7].ord and data[8,4].unpack with no length check, so a 7-byte payload gives nil.ord. fetch (fastimage.rb:293-298) rescues only the listed fetch/parse errors, not NoMethodError, so it reaches the caller.
claim: A short JFIF APP0 segment makes FastImage.resolution raise NoMethodError even with raise_on_failure false.
evidence: `data = @stream.read(length)` uses the segment's declared length. Once `data[0, 5] == "JFIF\0"` matches, `data[7].ord` and `data[8, 4].unpack("nn")` run with no length check. A declared length of 7 to 11 bytes makes `data[7]` or the slice nil, so the call raises NoMethodError. `fetch` (fastimage.rb:293-298) only rescues the listed fetch/parse errors (CannotParseImage, EOFError, etc.), so NoMethodError reaches the user. A length field under 2 makes `read(-n)` return nil, and `data[0,5]` raises the same way.

reason: read_rational_resolution (exif.rb:247-268) does `next if skip_amount < 0` on a forward-only stream. A rational stored before the IFD is skipped. When X and Y share one offset, reading X moves past it and Y is skipped, so tiff.rb:468 returns nil.
claim: TIFF/EXIF X/YResolution rationals stored before the current stream position, or sharing one offset, are silently dropped, so resolution comes back nil.
evidence: `read_rational_resolution` computes `skip_amount = absolute_pos - @stream.pos` and does `next if skip_amount < 0`. The stream only moves forward, so any rational offset before the current position is skipped without a value. Nothing records or reports this, and no fixture covers that layout ("test.dng" is expected to be nil without explanation).

reason: fastimage.gemspec:7 declares >= 1.9.2. exif.rb:19 adds `parse_resolution: false` and jpeg.rb:51 adds `&.`, and a grep of lib/ finds no earlier use of either, so requiring the gem on Ruby 1.9.2-2.2 now fails with SyntaxError. Lowered from high to medium: CI (.github/workflows/test.yml) already tests nothing below 2.3, and those runtimes are long EOL.
claim: Keyword-argument syntax (Ruby 2.0) and safe navigation (Ruby 2.3) break loading on older Rubies that the gemspec still allows.
evidence: fastimage.gemspec declares required_ruby_version >= 1.9.2, but Exif#initialize now uses keyword-argument syntax requiring Ruby 2.0, and jpeg.rb:51 uses safe navigation requiring Ruby 2.3. lib/fastimage/fastimage.rb unconditionally requires both parsers, so requiring fastimage on those older permitted runtimes fails with SyntaxError before any API can run.

reason: jpeg.rb:356 returns as soon as it finds any JFIF APP0, including units 0, before APP1 EXIF is read, and test3.jpg expects [[1,1], :no_units]. Whether EXIF should win is a spec choice that neither the code nor the packet settles. Lowered to low.
claim: JFIF density always beats EXIF X/YResolution, so a JFIF 0-units 1:1 placeholder hides a real EXIF DPI.
evidence: In the `MARKER_APP0` branch, `return [[x_density, y_density], unit_sym]` runs for any JFIF segment, including `JFIF_UNIT_ASPECT_RATIO` (mapped to :no_units). APP0 normally comes before APP1, so `exif_resolution` is never consulted. The locked fixture expects `"test3.jpg"=>[..., [[1, 1], :no_units]]`, so this precedence is never tested against a file that has both.

reason: parse_packets (fastimage.rb:474-489) raises CannotParseImage when the result is nil, and fetch swallows it, so @resolution stays undefined. resolution_units then calls resolution, which fetches again. This is a performance point and not a correctness defect, so it stays low.
claim: When there is no resolution, @resolution is never set, so every later resolution/resolution_units call fetches the image again.
evidence: `parse_resolution` returning nil makes `parse_packets` raise CannotParseImage, which `fetch` swallows, so `@resolution` stays undefined. `resolution_units` then does `resolution unless defined?(@resolution)`, which calls `fetch` again. `test_instance_resolution_returns_nil_for_format_without_resolution` calls both on test.png and so fetches it twice, but passes.

reason: ImageBase#resolution returns nil, parse_packets:488 raises CannotParseImage, and fetch:298 re-raises it when raise_on_failure is set, so the comment at fastimage.rb:186 is wrong for that option. This is a documentation mismatch.
claim: The docs say resolution returns nil when the image has no resolution data, but with raise_on_failure: true it raises CannotParseImage.
evidence: `ImageBase#resolution` returns nil, so `parse_packets` does `raise CannotParseImage`, and `fetch` re-raises it with `raise if @options[:raise_on_failure]`. The comment says "Returns nil if the image does not contain resolution information". No test exercises resolution with raise_on_failure.

reason: exif.rb:265-266 uses num.to_f / den while jpeg.rb uses unpack("nn"), png.rb unpack("NN") and bmp.rb unpack("l<l<"). The fixtures mix [[72,72]] and [[72.0,72.0]], and assert_equal treats them as equal. This is an API-consistency point.
claim: Resolution values are Floats for EXIF/TIFF and Integers for JFIF/PNG/BMP, and the tests can't tell the difference.
evidence: Exif uses `num.to_f / den`, while JFIF uses `unpack("nn")` and PNG uses `unpack("NN")`. The fixtures mix `[[72, 72], :inches]` (test.jpg) and `[[72.0, 72.0], :inches]` (test2.jpg), and `assert_equal` passes either way, so the test doesn't pin the type.

reason: None of the GoodFixtures resolution expectations in test/test.rb is :centimeters, so the JFIF_UNIT_CENTIMETERS and RESOLUTION_UNIT_CENTIMETERS branches never run. This is a test-coverage gap.
claim: The centimeters, EXIF no-units, BMP one-zero-axis and JPEG EXIF-only branches have no tests.
evidence: The resolution expectations in GoodFixtures contain only :inches, :meters and :no_units (from JFIF and PNG). No fixture produces :centimeters, so the `JFIF_UNIT_CENTIMETERS` and `RESOLUTION_UNIT_CENTIMETERS` branches in jpeg.rb and tiff.rb are never run.

reason: bmp.rb:131-132 does unpack("l<l<") and returns nil only when both are 0. Signed matches the BMP LONG field type, and whether a half-zero or negative value should give nil is not specified, so the code doesn't settle it as a defect.
claim: BMP pixels-per-metre values are read as signed and are rejected only when both are zero.
evidence: `x_ppm, y_ppm = data[38, 8].unpack("l<l<")` followed by `return nil if x_ppm == 0 && y_ppm == 0`.
